The change, from about 1769 to 1850, in which machines let Britain spin and weave cotton cloth as fine and cheap as India's. It was the first industry of the Industrial Revolution.

In the 1600s and 1700s light, bright Indian cotton cloth won over Europe (Indian calicoes win Europe). British makers could not match the fine Indian thread. A run of inventions changed that:

  • the spinning jenny of James Hargreaves, in the 1760s;
  • the water frame of Richard Arkwright, patented in 1769, run by water power in mills;
  • the spinning mule of Samuel Crompton, 1779, which made thread fine and strong;
  • steam power from the Watt engine and, later, the power loom.

Lancashire and its hub Manchester became the workshop for the world's cloth. The raw cotton came more and more from the American South, grown by enslaved people. Cheap British cloth then flooded India and hurt its weavers.

The historian Fernand Braudel argues that the cotton boom is what turned short spurts of growth into lasting growth.
